newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Yugoslavia invites OSCE to discuss Serbia poll.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia invites OSCE to discuss Serbia poll.

text.p: Europe's security forum, which sends observers to monitor elections, said on Friday Yugoslavia had invited the body to send a delegation to Belgrade to discuss disputed local elections.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said its outgoing chairman-in-office, Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti, had received the written request from Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic.
"The chairman-in-office of the OSCE welcomes this invitation and will give serious consideration to this request," the OSCE said in a statement.
"He believes this invitation could open up the possibility for dialogue. He will respond to the request soon."
Milutinovic wrote that the invitation had been made "due to dissatisfaction with the election results and the protests staged by a part of the opposition", the statement said.
The OSCE delegation should "obtain true information on all the facts so that any reserve be eliminated in our relations with the international community", it added.

Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic has come under heavy criticism from the West, particularly the United States, over his refusal to accept opposition victories in local elections in Serbia on November 17.
The authorities overturned the results in Belgrade and other towns claimed by the opposition, citing unspecified "irregularities".
Thousands of people have poured on to the streets of Belgrade every day for the past three weeks in peaceful protests over the quashing of the opposition victories.

An OSCE spokeswoman said earlier the 54-member organisation, which joins all European nations with the United States and Canada, would have no problem sending a delegation to Belgrade despite Yugoslavia's suspension from the body.
Yugoslavia -- comprising Serbia and Montenegro -- had its membership of the OSCE suspended in 1992 after Belgrade was accused of stoking the war in neighbouring Bosnia.
But she cautioned that the conditions of the invitation would have to be studied before OSCE experts left for Belgrade.

Milutinovic's request comes after an exchange of letters between Milosevic and U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and a visit to Belgrade on Thursday by Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.
Milosevic has proposed that the OSCE check the November vote in which the Zajedno opposition said the socialists suffered their worst defeat in 50 years of unbroken rule.
But one Western diplomatic source in Vienna said the OSCE should tread carefully to avoid being manipulated by the Serbian president.
The source said it was highly unlikely OSCE experts could properly verify a vote which took place almost a month ago.
"Anything could have happened to the ballots in that time," the source said. "Checking the election in that way would serve no purpose."

If OSCE experts do decide to meet Milosevic, they may propose that the election should be re-run with a full team of OSCE observers to monitor the poll, a diplomatic source said, giving Milosevic a possible face-saving way out of the conflict.
